'Elite traders' on WhatsApp post screenshots of R10 000 becoming R250 000 in weeks and urge you to 'top up' before the window closes. Legitimate growth takes time, regulation and visible paperwork. It's boring next to the story.

In South Africa: check FSCA warnings, ask for the FSP number and verify it at fsca.co.za, call the institution on its official switchboard (not the number the salesperson gives you), and never move money to a random personal account. If recruiting members pays more than the 'returns', you're looking at a pyramid, not an asset.

strings:

1. Cash buffer: Hold 1-2 years of living expenses in cash or money market. Draw from this during market downturns, giving equities time to recover without forced selling.

2. Bucket strategy: Divide the portfolio into short-term (cash, 1-3 years), medium-term (bonds and income assets, 3-7 years), and long-term (equities, 7+ years) buckets. Replenish the short-term bucket from the medium-term when markets are up.

3. Flexible withdrawals: Reduce withdrawals in bad years (spend less, draw less). Even a 10% reduction in withdrawals in a down year significantly extends portfolio longevity.

4. Living annuity vs guaranteed annuity: A guaranteed annuity transfers sequence risk to the insurer in exchange for surrendering capital. A living annuity retains flexibility but exposes the retiree to sequence risk. Many advisors recommend a blend.

key:
strings:

1. EBITDA Multiple (earnings-based): The most common for operating businesses. Value = EBITDA × industry multiple. SA SME multiples range from 2-5× EBITDA (vs 8-15× for listed companies). A profitable engineering firm with R2m EBITDA might sell for R6-8m (3-4× EBITDA). Factors increasing the multiple: recurring revenue, diversified customer base, management team not dependent on owner, strong growth trajectory.

2. Discounted Cash Flow (DCF): Project future free cash flows, discount back at a risk-adjusted rate (WACC). More theoretically correct but highly sensitive to assumptions. Mainly used for larger businesses or by financial advisors during due diligence.

3. Net Asset Value (NAV): Assets minus liabilities at market value. Used for asset-heavy businesses (property companies, mining, manufacturing). Often the floor value, a going concern should be worth more than its parts.

strings:

1. Harvesting losses: If you have unrealised losses in your portfolio, realise them in the same tax year as a large gain. Losses offset gains rand-for-rand before the inclusion rate applies.

2. Spreading disposals across tax years: The annual exclusion is use-it-or-lose-it. If you plan to sell a large position, staggering sales over multiple years uses multiple R40 000 exclusions.

3. TFSA wrapper: Assets inside a Tax-Free Savings Account have zero CGT, ever. Holding growth assets (equity ETFs) in your TFSA permanently eliminates CGT on those assets.

4. Donation to PBO: Donating an appreciated asset directly to a Section 18A public benefit organisation is not subject to CGT and generates a tax deduction up to 10% of taxable income.

key:
strings:

1. Inter vivos trust: Transfer appreciating assets into a trust now. Future growth falls outside your estate. The transfer triggers CGT now (one-time cost) but removes ongoing growth from estate duty calculations.

2. Life assurance (Section 3(3)(a)): A life policy where the estate is the beneficiary is included in the dutiable estate but the insurer pays the duty. These policies are built to fund estate duty, premiums are effectively pre-paying your estate duty in installments.

3. Spousal bequests to maximise portability: Structuring your will so the full estate goes to your spouse defers all duty to the second death, by which time abatements may have changed, or the surviving spouse's estate may be structured differently.

4. Donations during lifetime: Gifts of up to R100 000/year are free from Donations Tax. Over 20 years, R2 million can be transferred outside your estate, saving R400 000 in estate duty.

1. Sole Proprietor: No separation between you and the business. All profits taxed as personal income (up to 45%). Unlimited personal liability. Zero setup cost. Works for freelancers under R1m turnover.

2. Private Company (Pty Ltd): Separate legal entity. 27% corporate tax rate. Personal liability protection (limited). Requires CIPC registration. Ideal for businesses above R500k turnover.

3. Personal Service Provider (PSP): A Pty Ltd where 80%+ of income comes from services to one or two clients. SARS taxes PSPs at the 28-45% rate (not the 27% corporate rate), this is a trap many contractors fall into.

4. Small Business Corporation (SBC): A Pty Ltd qualifying for reduced tax rates. Gross income under R20 million. No shareholder may hold shares in another company. Tax rate: 0% on first R95 750, then 7%-27% on tiers. For qualifying SMEs, this saves substantial tax.

Anchoring: the first price you see reshapes how you judge every price after it. A R5 000 jacket makes a R2 000 one feel 'cheap'. Even when R2 000 is still a lot.

Sunk cost fallacy: continuing something because of money already spent, even when it no longer makes sense. 'I've paid for the gym, so I'll keep going even though I never do': versus cancelling and stopping the future waste. Money that's already gone should never drive your next decision.

Duration measures how sensitive a bond's price is to interest rate changes. A bond with a duration of 5 years will change in price by approximately 5% for every 1% change in interest rates.

Long-duration bonds (10-20 years) are more sensitive to rate changes. Short-duration bonds (1-3 years) are less sensitive.

SA context:

  • RSA Retail Bonds: no duration risk, you hold to maturity and the price is locked. Perfect for risk-averse investors.
  • Bond ETFs (Satrix Bond ETF, NewFunds GOVI ETF): hold a mix of government bonds. Have duration risk but also capital gain potential when rates fall.

For a buy-and-hold investor, duration risk is mainly psychological. For investors who need to sell before maturity, it's a real risk.

Gross Profit Margin: (Revenue - Cost of Goods Sold) ÷ Revenue. Measures how much you retain before overheads. A retail business at 25% GP margin is normal. A software business at 70%+ is normal. Compare to your industry benchmark.

EBITDA Margin: Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortisation ÷ Revenue. The cleanest measure of operational profitability. Used in business valuations (see next lesson).

Current Ratio: Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities. Above 1.5 = healthy. Below 1 = potential liquidity crisis, you may not be able to pay bills in 12 months.

Debtor Days: (Debtors ÷ Revenue) × 365. How long customers take to pay. 30 days is standard; 90+ days is a cash flow problem. Every day of debtor days = revenue sitting uncollected.

Net Profit Margin: Net profit ÷ Revenue. After all costs including tax. Most healthy SMEs: 8-20%.

Guaranteed annuity: Fixed monthly income for life. No investment risk. Income never runs out. Less flexible.

Living annuity: You control drawdown (2.5-17.5%). Investment risk remains with you. Can run out if drawdown is too high or markets perform poorly.

Most retirees benefit from a hybrid - guaranteed annuity for living costs, living annuity for discretionary spending and estate preservation.

Hedonic adaptation is the return to your usual level of happiness after a change. The new car thrills you for weeks, then becomes the car, which is why the next upgrade always feels necessary. Experiences resist it better than possessions, because they become memories rather than background. The strongest counters: bank part of every raise before adapting to it, space out treats so they stay treats, and deliberately notice what you already have.

Herd mentality is the pull to do what everyone else is doing. Our brains read a moving crowd as proof the direction is right. FOMO (fear of missing out) is its emotional engine.

The problem: the crowd usually arrives late, after prices have already run, and buys just as early holders sell. Protect yourself with three questions. Do I understand what I'm buying? Would I buy it if no one was talking about it? Can I explain how it makes a return?, and a rule to wait 48 hours before acting.

Included in your estate (dutiable):

  • Property, vehicles, investments in your name
  • Business interests (shares in Pty Ltd, partnership interest)
  • Retirement funds, only the after-tax lump sum amount payable to your estate (not nominated beneficiaries)
  • Life insurance policies where the estate is the beneficiary

Excluded from your estate:

  • Retirement fund proceeds paid to nominated beneficiaries (not the estate), these bypass estate duty entirely
  • Life policies payable to nominated beneficiaries (Section 3(3)(a) policies on which estate duty has already been accounted for)
  • Assets in a properly established inter vivos trust (owned by the trust, not you)

Beneficiary nominations on your pension, provident fund, and RA are therefore estate planning tools, not just administrative forms.

Lifestyle inflation is when every income increase is matched by a spending increase. You earn more but never build wealth. Sipho earns R20k and spends R19k; promoted to R30k, he upgrades the flat, car and subscriptions and now spends R29k. Still saving just R1k.

The fix is a rule you set in advance: when a raise lands, save at least half of the increase before upgrading anything. Wealth lives in the gap between what you earn and what you spend, protect the gap.

Loss aversion is the single biggest force in behavioral finance. Psychologists Kahneman and Tversky found that the emotional pain of losing R100 is approximately twice as strong as the pleasure of gaining R100.

This asymmetry causes rational people to make irrational financial decisions:

  • Holding onto losing investments too long, hoping to 'break even' before selling
  • Selling winning investments too early to 'lock in' gains before they disappear
  • Avoiding volatile assets entirely, even when long-term returns would be superior
  • Not rebalancing a portfolio because it means realising losses

Dropping cover in retirement is the worst time to do it: rejoining brings waiting periods and a permanent late-joiner penalty. Downgrade instead, and keep membership continuous. PMBs apply to every registered option. The most commonly ignored cost is frail care, which schemes largely don't cover.

Mental accounting is the tendency to treat money differently based on its origin or designated purpose, even though money is fungible (one rand is identical to any other rand).

Common examples:

  • Spending a bonus more freely than regular salary ('it's extra money')
  • Paying interest on a credit card while having savings sitting in a low-interest account ('that money is for emergencies')
  • Treating gambling winnings as 'free money' to be spent recklessly
  • Being stingy with cash but free with a credit card ('it doesn't feel like real money')

Mental accounting is why people simultaneously carry expensive debt and maintain large low-interest savings, a mathematically suboptimal combination.

Used deliberately, though, named goal accounts make the same bias work for you.

Overconfidence bias: Most people rate their driving, investing, and decision-making abilities as 'above average', which is statistically impossible for the majority. In investing, overconfidence causes excessive trading, under-diversification, and taking on more risk than your actual skill warrants.

Academic research consistently shows that individual investors who trade most actively achieve the worst net returns, because transaction costs and the pattern of buying high/selling low compound over time. The least active investors (who do nothing) typically outperform active traders.

Recency bias: The brain weights recent events heavily and assumes current trends will continue. After 3 years of strong JSE returns, investors expect strong returns. After a crash, they expect further falls. Both extrapolations are wrong more often than right.

Raising equity exposure after a run, or abandoning markets after a crash. Hindsight bias then convinces us we saw it coming, manufacturing confidence we never earned. The honest response: diversify, automate, and write predictions down before the outcome is known.

Present bias is the tendency to overvalue an immediate reward over a larger future one. It's why you know you should save but still spend. Economists call the underlying mechanism hyperbolic discounting. The future gets steeply 'discounted' the moment now is on the table.

The most powerful counter isn't more willpower. It's removing the in-the-moment decision. Automate the saving (a debit order on payday) so the money moves before you can spend it.

Public liability covers third-party injury or property damage. Often a procurement requirement before corporates will contract with you. Professional indemnity covers claims that your advice or work caused a client financial loss, and it applies to any professional service, not just doctors and lawyers. Replacement ratio: planners target about 70-80% of your final salary as retirement income. You need less than your full salary once saving stops and work costs fall.

The 4% rule: you can sustainably draw about 4% of your portfolio a year, so capital needed = annual income ÷ 0.04. Need R30 000/month (R360 000/year)? That's R9 million. The other lever is time: starting early lets compounding do the heavy lifting.

Risk capacity: How much risk you CAN take based on time horizon, income stability, and emergency fund.

Risk tolerance: How much risk you're EMOTIONALLY comfortable with.

Both matter. A 25-year-old with stable income and emergency fund has high capacity. But if they can't sleep during market dips, their tolerance is low. The right portfolio respects both.

SEFA (Small Enterprise Finance Agency): Government-backed loans from R10 000 to R15 million. Cheaper than bank rates, designed for SMEs that don't qualify for commercial bank loans. Black-owned and women-owned businesses get priority.

IDC (Industrial Development Corporation): R1m-R1 billion in loans and equity. Focus: manufacturing, agriculture, tourism, green economy. Longer terms, more flexible than banks.

DTI Incentives (now DTIC): Manufacturing Development Incentive (MDI), Support Programme for Industrial Innovation (SPII), Aquaculture Development, Tourism Support Programme. Some are grants (non-repayable) for qualifying businesses.

NDA (National Development Agency): Grants for NPOs and community-based organisations.

Key insight: Most SA entrepreneurs never apply for government incentives. The process is bureaucratic but the money is non-dilutive (you don't give up equity). For capital-intensive businesses, a DTIC grant or IDC loan can make a real difference.

Sole proprietor: no separation from you, profit taxed at your marginal rate (up to 45%), unlimited personal liability, zero setup cost. Pty Ltd: a separate legal entity with limited liability and 27% company tax (qualifying small companies, turnover under R20m, get reduced SBC rates).

Two traps to know: a Personal Service Provider (a Pty Ltd earning 80%+ from one or two clients for personal services) is taxed at individual rates, not 27%. And shares in your company sit inside your estate, while trust assets don't, which is why advanced structures often pair a trading company with a family trust that holds the shares.

It never promises that giving guarantees wealth, and teaching that it does burdens exactly the people least able to carry it.

Provisional tax: the self-employed pay in two estimates a year (around end of August and end of February). Rule of thumb: set aside 25-35% of every payment received; that's your future tax bill, not spending money.

A bond is a debt instrument. When you buy a bond, you are lending money to the issuer (a government or company) in exchange for:

  1. Regular interest payments (called the coupon) at a fixed rate
  2. Return of your principal (the amount you lent) at maturity (the end date)

Example: You buy a R10 000 RSA Retail Bond with a 10% coupon and 5-year maturity. You receive R1 000/year in interest. After 5 years, you get your R10 000 back.

Bond issuers: SA Government (RSA Retail Bonds, Treasury bonds), SOEs (Eskom bonds), municipalities, and listed companies (corporate bonds).

The common answer is a hybrid: guarantee your essential expenses, keep the discretionary portion flexible. Both incomes are taxed as income.

A business can be profitable but have no cash. This is the most common cause of SME failure in SA.

Example: Priya's catering company bills R500 000 in March. Customers pay in 60 days (May). She pays wages, food, and rent now. The income statement shows R500 000 revenue. Her bank account shows -R200 000. She is profitable and cash-flow negative simultaneously.

The cash conversion cycle: How long between paying for inputs and collecting from customers. Shorter = better. Strategies to shorten: require deposits, offer early-payment discounts, delay supplier payments within agreed terms, factor debtors (sell invoices to a financier at a discount).

Rule: Never confuse your accounting profit with your bank balance. Run a weekly cash flow forecast for the next 13 weeks. If it turns negative, you need to act months before the crisis hits.

A classic mental accounting error: keeping R30 000 in a savings account earning 7% while carrying R30 000 in credit card debt at 22%. The logic: 'I can't touch my savings - those are for emergencies.' But you're losing 15% net by holding both simultaneously.

The rational action: use savings to clear 22% debt, then rebuild savings at 7%. The emergency fund is rebuilt at 7% instead of costing you 15%.

A credit score of 550 vs 720 is not just a number, it translates directly into rands over a lifetime:

Home loan example (R1 000 000, 20 years):

  • Score 720+ → prime - 0.5% → 10.75% → monthly repayment: R9 800, total repaid: R2 352 000
  • Score 550 → prime + 1.5% → 12.75% → monthly repayment: R11 400, total repaid: R2 736 000
  • Difference: R384 000 over 20 years, purely due to credit score

A good credit score is worth more than most investment accounts for many South Africans. Building it is as important as building savings.

A home loan (a bond in SA) is a secured loan. The property is collateral, so if you stop paying, the bank can repossess it.

Key terms: LTV (loan ÷ value. Lower is safer for the bank, often a better rate); Prime rate (set by the SARB's repo rate; your bond is prime ± a spread for your credit risk); First Home Finance (formerly FLISP: a government subsidy for first-time buyers earning R3 501–R22 000/month that reduces your bond). Your actual rate depends on prime and your profile, so always stress-test against rate rises.

A Ponzi works in phases:

  1. Launch: Recruit early investors with promised high returns
  2. Pay early investors: Using new investors' money - builds credibility
  3. Growth phase: Early investors recruit community members (affinity fraud)
  4. Collapse: New money can't keep up with withdrawal requests - scheme collapses, most investors lose everything

Early investors may make money. Late investors (the majority) lose almost everything.

In SA, slow-paying clients (especially large corporates) cause thousands of small business failures annually.

A shareholders agreement governs the relationship between shareholders, what happens when someone wants to leave, dies, goes bankrupt, or you disagree fundamentally. Without one, the default Companies Act rules apply, and they are rarely what you want.

Critical clauses every SA shareholders agreement needs:

  • Tag-along: If a majority shareholder sells, minority shareholders can join the sale on the same terms
  • Drag-along: Majority can force minority to sell if a buyer wants 100%
  • Right of first refusal: Before a shareholder sells to an outsider, existing shareholders get first right to buy at the same price
  • Deadlock resolution: When equal shareholders disagree on a fundamental decision, the mechanism to resolve it (buy-sell clause, mediation, arbitration)
  • Buyout on death/disability: What happens to shares if a shareholder dies or becomes incapacitated? Fund this with life and disability insurance.

A trust is not a company and not a person. It is a legal arrangement where a founder transfers assets to trustees, who hold and manage them for the benefit of beneficiaries. The trust owns the assets, not you personally.

Two main types in SA:

  • Inter vivos trust: Created during your lifetime. Used for asset protection, estate duty reduction, and family wealth continuity.
  • Testamentary trust: Created by your will on your death. Commonly used to protect inheritances for minor children.

The key insight: Because the trust owns assets, not you, those assets are not part of your estate when you die, meaning no estate duty on them. This is the primary reason high-net-worth South Africans use trusts.

Academic research (Fama-French, 1992 onward) identified specific characteristics, 'factors', that have historically delivered higher returns than the broad market over long periods. These are not tips or predictions. They are systematic, rules-based tilts.

The five factors with the strongest evidence:

  • Value: Cheap stocks (low price-to-book, price-to-earnings) outperform expensive ones over long periods
  • Size: Smaller companies have historically outperformed large caps
  • Momentum: Stocks that have risen over the past 6-12 months tend to continue rising in the short term
  • Quality: Profitable, low-debt companies with stable earnings outperform
  • Low Volatility: Lower-risk stocks have outperformed higher-risk stocks. The opposite of what CAPM predicts.

  • Gains from frequent trading = income tax. Occasional long-term sales = CGT (40% inclusion rate)

Non-declaration is tax evasion with criminal consequences.

One ETF purchase gives you instant diversification across hundreds or thousands of companies. They're special because: typically low TERs (often well under 1%), transparent holdings, liquid on the JSE, and tax-efficient inside a TFSA. Several licensed SA platforms let you buy them with small amounts.

Anele saved R40 000 in a notice account for a car deposit nine months away. Her colleague put the same amount in volatile single shares for the same goal. When prices dipped 18%, only one of them could still buy the car without delay.

Time horizon is the gap between today and when you must spend the money. Under two years usually favours stability; five years or more can carry more growth assets, if you won't panic-sell. Mixing up timelines is how people sell low right before prices recover.

Where you must sell, do it inside a TFSA or retirement fund, where there's no CGT.

At retirement, you must convert your retirement savings into income. Two primary choices:

Guaranteed (life) annuity: Fixed monthly income for life, regardless of how long you live. No investment risk. Income never runs out. Non-negotiable - you can't change it once purchased.

Living annuity: You remain invested. Draw 2.5-17.5% per year. Flexible income. Investment risk stays with you. Can run out. Remaining capital passes to heirs.

Base cost is what you paid for the asset (purchase price + broker fees + improvement costs for property). It sets the size of your gain.

Pre-valuation date assets: If you owned assets before 1 October 2001 (CGT's introduction date), the base cost can be determined using the market value on that date, not the original purchase price. This often dramatically reduces gains on long-held shares or property.

What SARS expects: Keep all contract notes (share trades), transfer duty receipts, improvement invoices, and estate agent agreements permanently. SARS can audit 5 years back but has no time limit for fraudulent returns. A shoebox with no records is a tax liability waiting to happen.

Beyond the distribution formula, dying without a will causes:

  • The Master's Office appoints an executor: Often a bank trust company charging 3.5% + VAT on the gross estate value. On a R3 million estate, that is R139 650 in fees, vs under R20 000 if you nominated your own executor and fee.
  • Delays of 12-24+ months: Without a clear mandate, the winding-up process drags through the Master's Office.
  • Family conflict: The formula ignores relationships, promises, and practical needs. Minor children's inheritance is managed by the Guardian's Fund, not your surviving spouse.
  • Guardian's Fund trap: If your minor children inherit, the money goes into the Government Guardian's Fund, earning below-market interest, until they turn 18.

Bitcoin cycles in SA perfectly illustrate FOMO investing:

  • 2020: Few people notice Bitcoin rising
  • Late 2021: Bitcoin near $69k, mainstream media coverage, FOMO peak
  • 2022: Bitcoin falls 70%, FOMO buyers lose most of their investment
  • 2023-24: Bitcoin recovers to new highs while 2021 FOMO buyers are still at a loss

Those who bought based on FOMO in 2021 suffered; those who held through the cycle based on conviction eventually recovered. The difference was motivation: FOMO vs research.

Bond funds have no maturity date, so their value keeps moving.

Buyers will discount (lower) your asking price for these red flags, which are all correctable before a sale:

  • Key person dependency: If the owner IS the business (all relationships, all knowledge), the business is worth far less without them. Solution: document processes, introduce the management team to key clients, create a 12-month transition plan.
  • Customer concentration: If 60%+ of revenue comes from one client, the buyer is buying a client relationship, not a business. Solution: diversify before selling.
  • Unclean books: Personal expenses through the company, informal transactions, mixed accounts. Solution: 2-3 years of clean, audited or reviewed annual financial statements increase both value and buyer confidence.
  • No contracts: Verbal agreements with key customers or suppliers. Buyers need contractual revenue. Solution: formalise all key relationships into written agreements.

For individuals: 40% of the gain is included in taxable income (called the 'inclusion rate'). On a gain of R100 000, R40 000 is added to your income and taxed at your marginal rate. At 36%: effective CGT = R14 400.

Capital Gains Tax is not a separate tax in South Africa. It's a top-up to income tax. When you dispose of an asset (sell, gift, die, or emigrate), SARS includes a portion of the profit in your taxable income for that year.

The inclusion rates for 2024/25:

  • Individuals: 40% of the gain is included in taxable income
  • Companies: 80% included
  • Trusts: 80% included (45% flat rate × 80% = effective 36%)

An individual in the 45% bracket pays effectively 18% CGT (45% × 40%). Not 45%. This distinction matters.

Commercial banks lend against trading history, financial statements, security and director surety. A strong plan alone rarely does it. State support now runs through SEDFA, which merged SEFA, SEDA and the CBDA in October 2024; the NEF has a separate B-BBEE mandate. Debt must be repaid but preserves ownership; equity needs no repayment but sells a permanent share of every future rand. Retained profit and customer deposits remain the cheapest capital of all.

Consider: outstanding debt (bond + car), income gap during recovery, home modification costs, and specialist treatment co-payments that medical aid won't cover.

Compare renting vs buying the same R1 500 000 home over 20 years. Buying (R150k deposit, a bond plus rates, insurance and maintenance, ~R120k upfront costs) leaves you with a paid-off asset, but you've paid far more out of pocket along the way. Renting and investing the monthly difference (and the upfront costs) at ~10%/year can build a comparable or larger portfolio.

In many SA markets, a disciplined renter-investor ends up with equal or greater wealth, but only if they actually invest the savings. Property's edge is leverage, lifestyle and forced saving. Neither answer is universally right; it depends on your city, returns, timeline and discipline.

A representative must: complete the required recognised qualification (generally within six years of DOFA), pass the relevant regulatory examination (RE5) (generally within the required period from DOFA), and complete class-of-business and product-specific training before rendering advice in that product.

Until these are met, the person works under supervision.

R10 000 at 10% a year: R11 000 after year 1, R16 105 after 5 years, R25 937 after 10, R67 275 after 20, R174 494 after 30, and you did nothing after year 1. Time did the work. R500/month for 20 years at ~10% becomes over R400 000, from about R120 000 of your own contributions.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek out and give more weight to information that confirms your existing beliefs, while ignoring or dismissing information that challenges them. In investing, it causes investors to: only read positive news about assets they own, dismiss valid warnings as 'fake news', and hold failing investments far too long.

Credit repair is not instant, but it is systematic. Here is what SA credit bureaus retain and when it falls off your record:

  • Late payments: 1-2 years (on most bureau records)
  • Defaults: 1-2 years after account is settled
  • Debt review/administration: Removed within 5 business days of clearance certificate
  • Judgements: 5 years or until rescinded, whichever is sooner
  • Enquiries (hard checks): 12 months

The fastest path from a damaged score to a good score (620+): clear all defaults, pay everything on time from this moment, reduce utilisation, and wait. Most people see significant improvement within 12-18 months of consistent behaviour.

Crude oil is priced globally in US dollars. South Africa imports most of its fuel. Each litre of petrol you buy is affected by: (1) the global oil price in dollars, and (2) the rand/dollar exchange rate.

A 10% rand weakening increases petrol costs by approximately 10% - regardless of what happens to the oil price. Every R1 weakening against the dollar adds approximately R0.25-R0.40/litre to the pump price.

'Not your keys, not your coins': holdings on an exchange are a claim against a company, so long-term positions belong in self-custody. Use app-based 2FA, never SMS, SIM swap fraud is common here, and never share a seed phrase.

Cryptocurrency is digital money secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain, a shared public ledger maintained by thousands of computers, with no single bank or government in control. Bitcoin (2009) was the first; there are now thousands, most of them worthless.

It IS a volatile, speculative asset class with real historical returns, and it's taxable in SA. It ISN'T guaranteed, anonymous (the blockchain is traceable), or a day-to-day replacement for the rand.

DALBAR's annual Quantitative Analysis of Investor Behaviour consistently shows that the average investor earns significantly less than the market index, not because markets fail but because of behavioural mistakes:

  • Buying after strong performance (recency bias)
  • Selling during crashes (loss aversion)
  • Switching funds frequently (overconfidence and transaction costs)

Over 20 years, the average US equity investor has earned roughly 4-5% annually while the S&P 500 returned 9-10%. The gap, 4-5% per year compounded over 20 years, represents enormous missed wealth.

SA equivalent: The JSE Capped SWIX has returned approximately 12-14% annually over the last 20 years. Most active SA unit trust investors have significantly underperformed this.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that humans feel the pain of a loss roughly twice as intensely as the pleasure of an equal gain. Losing R1 000 hurts about twice as much as gaining R1 000 feels good.

That asymmetry quietly wrecks returns: people hold losing investments too long hoping to break even, panic-sell at market bottoms, or avoid investing at all. The rational response is to evaluate an investment on its future prospects, if you wouldn't buy it today, the price you paid shouldn't keep you in it.

Debarment must follow a fair process. The FSP must: give the representative notice of the intention to debar and the reasons; give them a reasonable opportunity to respond/make representations; consider that response; and, if it proceeds, notify the person of the debarment and their right to reconsideration/appeal.

The FSP must then notify the FSCA and update its register. The FSCA maintains a public record so other FSPs can check before appointing someone.

It simplifies management and can reduce total interest - but ONLY works if you don't accumulate new debt on the cleared accounts.

Debt consolidation means one new loan to pay off several smaller debts, so you make a single monthly payment.

When it helps: a lower rate, a lower total payment, simpler management. When it hurts: stretching the term can mean more interest overall, and many people clear their cards then run them up again.

Decades of research (Fama-French onward) identified factors. Characteristics that have earned a premium over the market: value (cheap), size (smaller), momentum (recent winners), quality (profitable, low-debt) and low volatility. These are systematic, rules-based tilts, not tips.

'Smart-beta' ETFs deliver factor exposure cheaply (~0.2-0.5% vs 1.5-2.5% for active). The discipline: hold factors as long-term tilts, combine uncorrelated ones, and accept that any factor can lag for years without being broken.

Pre-commitment is the key - willpower fails once money lands.

Diversification means spreading your investments across different assets so one bad investment can't wipe you out.

A diversified portfolio might look like: 30% SA shares (a JSE ETF), 30% global shares (e.g. an S&P 500 ETF), 20% bonds, 10% property (a REIT), 10% cash. The point isn't to maximise your best case. It's to make sure no single failure can ruin you.

Over time, your average cost per unit is automatically lower than the average price - you benefit from volatility rather than fear it.

Don't borrow to grow if:

  • Your current cash flow can't service the debt payments comfortably
  • You're borrowing to cover operating losses (not growth)
  • The expected return from the growth doesn't exceed the cost of the debt
  • You haven't tested the market and proven demand exists

Most SA small business failures follow taking on debt before the business model was proven.

Donations tax applies when you give away assets or cash exceeding R100 000 per year. Rate: 20% on donations up to R30 million, 25% above. Exempt: Donations to spouses, approved charities, and bona fide maintenance to dependants.

Practical example: giving R150 000 cash to your adult child = R50 000 taxable gift × 20% = R10 000 donations tax (paid by the donor).

Dread disease cover (also called critical illness cover) pays a tax-free lump sum if you're diagnosed with a serious illness, even if you survive and recover.

Conditions typically include cancer, heart attack, stroke and kidney failure. In SA, treatment for a serious illness can run to hundreds of thousands of rands, and even with medical aid the shortfalls and lost income can wipe out savings. The lump sum is yours to use as you choose: unlike income protection, which replaces your monthly salary.

During the Steinhoff collapse (2017), thousands of individual SA investors watched shares fall from R95 to R2 over two months. Many held, hoping for a recovery to break even. By 2024, shares traded at under R1.

The break-even trap is expensive because:

  • Capital locked in a loser can't earn returns in better investments
  • The original purchase price is a sunk cost, irrelevant to the decision today
  • Ask instead: 'If I received this cash today, would I buy these shares at the current price?' If no, sell.

This reframe (the 'sell or hold' test) removes the anchor of your purchase price from the decision.

Dying without a valid will is called dying intestate. When this happens, the Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987 distributes your estate, not your wishes.

The intestate formula:

  • If you are married with children: spouse gets R250 000 or a child's share (whichever is greater). Children share the rest.
  • If you have children but no spouse: children share everything equally
  • If you have a spouse but no children: spouse gets everything
  • If you have neither: parents, then siblings, then further relatives

Cohabiting partners (unmarried) receive nothing under intestate succession, regardless of how long they lived together or what was jointly purchased.

Dying without a valid will is called dying intestate. When this happens, the Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987 distributes your estate, not your wishes.

The intestate formula:

  • If you are married with children: spouse gets R250 000 or a child's share (whichever is greater). Children share the rest.
  • If you have children but no spouse: children share everything equally
  • If you have a spouse but no children: spouse gets everything
  • If you have neither: parents, then siblings, then further relatives

Cohabiting partners (unmarried) receive nothing under intestate succession, regardless of how long they lived together or what was jointly purchased.

Dying without a valid will is dying intestate: the Intestate Succession Act distributes your estate by a fixed formula, not your wishes. Cohabiting (unmarried) partners receive nothing automatically, minor children's inheritances can go to the state Guardian's Fund, and the Master appoints an executor (often a bank charging up to 3.5% + VAT).

A valid will needs only to be signed before two competent witnesses present together, but a witness who is also a beneficiary forfeits that bequest, so keep them separate. Name your own executor and negotiate the fee in advance.

Each block is cryptographically linked to the one before it, and thousands of computers hold copies, so altering history breaks every block after it and the network rejects your version. Transactions are pseudonymous, not anonymous: the ledger is permanently public, which makes blockchain more traceable than cash. It solves one problem, transferring value without a trusted middleman, and it isn't automatically cheaper or faster than a local instant payment.

Estate duty is a tax on the total value of your estate when you die. It is a significant wealth transfer tax, and probably the least understood.

2024/25 rates:

  • 20% on dutiable estate up to R30 million
  • 25% on dutiable estate above R30 million

The R3.5 million abatement: Every individual gets a R3.5 million deduction before estate duty applies. Your first R3.5 million passes estate-duty-free.

Spousal rollover: Assets left to a surviving spouse are fully exempt from estate duty, the tax is deferred to when the surviving spouse dies. Unused abatement from the first death rolls over to the surviving spouse (portability of abatement).

Retirement funds and life policies paid to nominated beneficiaries bypass the estate entirely. The classic trap is liquidity: duty, fees and debts fall due in cash within about 12 months, while most wealth is illiquid, which is what an estate-pegged (s3(3)(a)) life policy is designed to solve.

key:
strings:

Estate duty, executor fees, outstanding debt, and transfer costs must usually be paid within 12 months of death. The problem: most wealth is illiquid (property, retirement funds, business interests).

Example: Zanele's estate: R6m property, R2m RA (to be taxed), R500k car, R300k investments. Net estate = R8.8m. Estate duty = approximately R1.06m. Executor fees (3.5%) = R308 000. Total liability: ~R1.37 million due in cash within 12 months.

Her liquid investments (R300k) are far short. The executor must either:

  • Sell the property under time pressure (often below market value)
  • Accept a Section 35 SARS payment arrangement
  • Fund the shortfall via a Section 3(3)(a) estate-pegged life policy

Every business produces three core financial statements:

1. Income Statement (P&L): Shows revenue, costs, and profit over a period. Answers: 'Is the business making money?'

2. Balance Sheet: Shows assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time. Answers: 'What does the business own and owe?'

3. Cash Flow Statement: Shows actual cash moving in and out. Answers: 'Does the business have cash to survive?' (A business can be profitable but cash-flow negative, this is how profitable companies go bankrupt.)

Factor returns come with a catch: they can underperform for years. Value underperformed growth for the entire decade 2010-2020 before recovering strongly in 2021-2022. A disciplined investor who abandoned value in 2019 missed the recovery.

Key disciplines for factor investing:

  • Use factors as long-term tilts (10+ year horizon), not short-term trades
  • Combine uncorrelated factors (value + momentum, quality + low vol) to smooth underperformance periods
  • Keep factor exposure cheap, Smart Beta ETFs give factor exposure at 0.2-0.5% fees vs 1.5-2.5% for active funds that claim factor tilts
  • Accept that any factor can underperform for 3-5 years without it 'being broken'

  • Capital needed: R360 000 ÷ 4% = R9 million
  • At R9 million in investments, you can stop working - at any age

The FI number can be reached much earlier than traditional retirement age with high savings rates (50%+ of income).

For a will to be valid in South Africa it must:

  • Be in writing (handwritten or typed)
  • Be signed by the testator (you) at the end of the document and at the bottom of each page
  • Be signed in the presence of two competent witnesses, both present at the same time
  • Witnesses must sign in your presence and in the presence of each other
  • Witnesses must be 14+ years old and mentally competent
  • Critical rule: A witness (or their spouse) cannot be a beneficiary under the will. If they are, the bequest to them is void, the rest of the will stands.

You do not need a lawyer, notary, or commissioner of oaths to create a valid will. But professional drafting catches issues that can void or complicate a will years later.

Never scan investment or banking QR codes received via WhatsApp, even from apparent friends - their accounts may be compromised.

From 1 March 2017, SARS introduced Section 7C to prevent a widely-used scheme: individuals sold assets to their trust for a low purchase price on an interest-free loan account, effectively freezing the value in their estate.

Section 7C says: Any loan from you (a connected person) to a trust at below the official interest rate triggers Donations Tax on the interest 'forgone'. At repo rate 7.75%, a R10 million interest-free loan generates R775 000 in notional donations per year. After the R100 000 annual exclusion, R675 000 is subject to 20% Donations Tax = R135 000/year.

The impact: Many historic trust structures built before 2017 are now annual tax liabilities. Trustees and advisors need to either charge proper interest on loans, waive debt strategically, or restructure.

Savings Pot (1/3): one withdrawal per tax year (minimum R2 000), taxed as income: an emergency provision only. Retirement Pot (2/3): locked until retirement, no exceptions. Vested Pot: everything saved before 1 Sep 2024, under the old rules.

From cheapest to most expensive in terms of cost and control:

  1. Bootstrapping: Revenue funds growth. No dilution, no interest. Slow.
  2. Government grants and incentives: Free money, but slow, bureaucratic, and restrictive. Worth pursuing if your business qualifies.
  3. Debt (bank loans, asset finance): You pay interest but keep equity. Banks lend against assets or cash flow. SA SME lending rates: prime + 2-6%.
  4. Revenue-based financing: Funder takes a % of monthly revenue until repaid. Flexible for cash-flow businesses.
  5. Angel investors: Private individuals investing R500k-R5m for equity (10-25%). Bring expertise and networks.
  6. Venture capital: R5m-R100m+ for fast-growth businesses. Expect significant dilution (20-40%) and board control requirements.
  7. Private equity: Larger investments in established businesses, typically for majority control.

Funding runs from cheapest-in-control to most-dilutive: bootstrapping (self-funded, slow), government finance and grants (SEFA loans, IDC, DTIC grants, cheaper or non-dilutive but bureaucratic), debt (interest, but you keep your equity), and equity (angels, VC. Cash and expertise, but you give up ownership and some control).

The core trade-off: debt keeps ownership but must be repaid; equity shares the risk but dilutes you. And before any co-owner or investor comes in, a shareholders agreement (covering exits, disputes, deadlock and death) is non-negotiable.

Gains are taxed either as capital (CGT, max ~18% effective) or as revenue (your full marginal rate), intention and trading frequency decide which. Crypto-to-crypto swaps are disposals and must be valued in rands and declared, even though no rands changed hands. On a R120 000 gain, the R50 000 annual exclusion leaves R70 000, and 40% of that (R28 000) is added to taxable income. Export your transaction history every year.

Gross rental yield is annual rent ÷ price. R96 000 on a R1.2m flat is 8% gross. Net is what matters: rates, levies, insurance, maintenance, agent fees and vacant months routinely take a third of the rent. Buy-to-let is a small business, not passive income, and eviction is a months-long court process. A listed REIT gives property exposure with no tenants and same-day liquidity, but no leverage and no control.

Harry Markowitz's 1952 Nobel Prize-winning insight: you can combine assets that individually are risky into a portfolio that is less risky than any single asset, while maintaining return. This is the free lunch of diversification.

The key: correlation. When SA stocks fall, your US bonds may rise. When the JSE All Share drops 30%, global equity ETFs in rand terms may cushion the blow because global markets don't always move in lockstep with SA, and a weakening rand boosts offshore returns.

The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios that offer the highest expected return for each level of risk (standard deviation). Portfolios below the frontier are inefficient (you are taking more risk than necessary for the return you earn).

Have you noticed that R100 today doesn't buy as much as it did 5 years ago? That's because of inflation.

Inflation means the general increase in prices over time. In South Africa, the Reserve Bank aims to keep inflation between 3-6% per year.

This is why keeping cash under your mattress is a bad idea, it loses purchasing power every year!

Over 25 years of retirement, healthcare costs for a couple can exceed R5-10 million in total.

Hedonic adaptation is the psychological process by which we quickly return to a stable level of happiness regardless of positive or negative events. You buy the new car and feel amazing for 3 months - then it becomes the normal car you barely notice. You upgrade your apartment - within months it's just home.

This mechanism drives perpetual lifestyle inflation: always upgrading, always chasing the next happiness boost, never building lasting wealth.

Herd mentality is the tendency to follow the crowd in financial decisions - buying what everyone else is buying (cryptocurrency in 2021, property in 2007) without independent analysis. FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) amplifies this: watching others' apparent gains creates urgency to join.

Both biases have caused more wealth destruction in SA than almost any other psychological trap.

Here is something most investors get wrong: when interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall. When rates fall, bond prices rise.

Why this happens: Imagine you own a R10 000 bond paying 8% (R800/year). Interest rates then rise to 10%. New bonds now pay R1 000/year on the same R10 000. Your 8% bond is less attractive, who would pay R10 000 for it when they can get R1 000/year from a new bond? Your bond's market price must drop until its yield matches the new market rate.

This matters for bond ETFs and unit trusts, they hold bonds that are marked to market. During SA's 2022-2024 rate hike cycle, bond funds lost value even though the underlying coupons were still being paid.

If you work outside SA for a foreign employer for more than 183 days in a 12-month period (including at least 60 consecutive days), your foreign employment income is exempt from SA tax up to R1.25 million per year.

Above R1.25 million: The excess is taxed in SA. You may credit foreign tax paid against your SA liability.

Important 2020 amendment: Before 1 March 2020, all foreign employment income was fully exempt. SARS closed this loophole. Now only R1.25 million is exempt. Many South Africans working in the Gulf (where there is zero income tax) were significantly impacted.

  1. Call your bank's 24/7 fraud line immediately
  2. Freeze or cancel your cards via the banking app
  3. Do NOT contact the scammer (they may try to 'recover' money with further fraud)
  4. Document everything: screenshots, call recordings, WhatsApp history
  5. Report to SAPS and the FSCA

If your RA or pension fund is governed by Regulation 28 (most local funds are), it limits offshore exposure:

  • Maximum 45% offshore (increased from 30% in 2022)
  • Maximum 10% in Africa (excluding SA)
  • Maximum 25% in equities (listed and unlisted)

This means your RA cannot be 100% offshore, it must hold at least 55% SA assets. This is a government policy decision to keep retirement savings partly funding SA infrastructure.

Outside Regulation 28 (personal taxable investments and TFSA): No offshore limit. You can hold 100% global equity ETF in your TFSA if you choose. Many advisors recommend 50-75% offshore in the non-retirement portion of a SA investor's portfolio.

If your score is below 550 (poor), follow this sequence:

  1. Check your report for errors first. A significant percentage of SA credit reports contain inaccurate adverse information. Dispute anything incorrect immediately.
  2. Clear all outstanding defaults. Contact creditors directly, many accept settlements below the full amount. Get a settlement letter in writing and follow up to confirm bureau removal.
  3. Never miss another payment. One missed payment undoes months of rebuild. Set payment reminders or automate every account.
  4. Reduce utilisation below 30%. Pay down balances aggressively before applying for anything new.
  5. Do not apply for new credit. Each hard inquiry lowers your score. Wait until you've stabilised before seeking new credit.
  6. Consider a secured credit card. A retail bank account with a R2 000 temporary overdraft used and repaid monthly shows positive payment behaviour if your history is thin.

If your target allocation is 60% equities / 40% bonds, and equities surge 30% while bonds return 5%, your portfolio drifts to roughly 65/35. Rebalancing back to 60/40 forces you to sell equities (which have risen) and buy bonds (which are relatively cheap). This is systematic buying low and selling high.

Rebalancing discipline in SA:

  • Use annual or threshold-triggered rebalancing (e.g., when any asset class drifts more than 5% from target)
  • Within a TFSA, rebalancing is free, no CGT. In taxable accounts, rebalancing may trigger CGT. Prefer to rebalance using new contributions where possible.
  • Avoid over-rebalancing, transaction costs and CGT erode benefits of frequent rebalancing

Imagine two retirees, both with R5 million and a 10% average annual return over 20 years. Retiree A gets good returns early (25%, 20%) then bad later (-25%, -20%). Retiree B gets the exact reverse, bad early, good later.

They have identical average returns. But Retiree B, who faced large losses early while withdrawing living expenses, runs out of money 8 years before Retiree A.

This is sequence-of-returns risk, the order of returns matters enormously in retirement. A market crash in year 2 of retirement permanently depletes capital that would otherwise have compounded.

Imagine you start with 60% equities and 40% bonds. After a great year, equities return 25% and bonds return 5%. Your portfolio is now approximately 65% equities and 35% bonds, you've drifted from your target allocation and taken on more risk than intended.

Rebalancing means selling the outperformers and buying the underperformers to return to your target allocation. It feels counterintuitive, you're selling what's working, but it enforces the discipline of buy-low, sell-high.

How often to rebalance: Most evidence suggests annual rebalancing is sufficient. More frequent rebalancing generates unnecessary transaction costs and tax events.

Rebalancing means selling the outperformers and buying the underperformers to return to your target allocation. It feels counterintuitive, you're selling what's working, but it enforces the discipline of buy-low, sell-high.

How often to rebalance: Most evidence suggests annual rebalancing is sufficient. More frequent rebalancing generates unnecessary transaction costs and tax events.

In South Africa, families lose their homes and children leave school when a breadwinner dies without life cover. It's not a rare tragedy. It's the predictable outcome of skipping one product.

Life insurance pays a lump sum to your family if you die. If people depend on your income (a spouse, children, parents) you need it. A common rule of thumb: 10× your annual salary. Earning R300 000/year suggests about R3 million in cover.

In South Africa, selling assets to rebalance can trigger Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Tax-smart rebalancing minimises this:

  • Rebalance with new contributions: Instead of selling, direct new monthly investments into underweight asset classes. No sale = no CGT.
  • Use tax-advantaged accounts first: Rebalancing inside a Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) generates no CGT. Use TFSAs for your most active rebalancing.
  • Annual exclusion: Each individual has a R40 000 annual capital gain exclusion. Small rebalancing sales may fall within this exclusion.
  • Hold periods: Assets held over 3 years in a RA (Retirement Annuity) have no CGT on withdrawal, ideal for equity holdings.

Income retained in a South African trust is taxed at a flat 45%, with an 80% CGT inclusion (an effective 36% on gains) and no rebates or exclusions. So a trust is not an income-tax saver.

The planning tool is the conduit principle: income distributed to beneficiaries in the same tax year is taxed in their (often lower) hands instead. People use trusts mainly for estate planning and asset protection. Assets held in a trust fall outside your personal estate. Note s7C: interest-free loans to a trust are treated as ongoing donations.

Inflation and interest rates are locked in a perpetual tug-of-war. Understanding this relationship explains almost everything about why your grocery bill, petrol price, and bond repayment change over time.

CPI (Consumer Price Index): SA's measure of inflation, tracking a basket of goods and services. When CPI is above 6%, the SARB is under pressure to raise rates. When CPI is below 4.5%, the SARB has room to cut.

In 2022, SA CPI peaked at 7.8%, above the target ceiling. The MPC responded with 475 basis points of rate hikes over 18 months. By mid-2024, CPI had fallen to 5.4%, enabling the first cuts in four years.

Leave R100 000 in cash instead of investing and you quietly lose about R6 000 a year in buying power to inflation. After 10 years, that R100 000 buys what R55 000 used to. Doing nothing isn't safe. It's slow financial erosion.

Let's compare renting vs buying the same R1 500 000 property in South Africa over 20 years.

Buying scenario:

  • Deposit: R150 000 (10%)
  • Bond: R1 350 000 at 11.5% over 20 years = R14 560/month
  • Rates + insurance + maintenance: R3 500/month
  • Total monthly cost: R18 060
  • Upfront transaction costs: R120 000 (transfer + bond registration)
  • Total paid over 20 years: R4 454 400 + R270 000 upfront = R4 724 400
  • Property value at 6% growth: R4 813 000
  • Net asset gain: approximately R358 000 after repaying the bond

Renting and investing scenario:

  • Rent for similar property: R9 500/month (current rental yield)
  • Monthly saving vs buying: R8 560 - invest this at 10%/year
  • Also invest the R270 000 transaction costs at 10%/year
  • Total investment portfolio after 20 years: approximately R2 200 000

The result: In many SA markets, the renter who invests the difference ends up with comparable or greater wealth. The buyer has an asset but has paid far more out of pocket. Neither answer is universally right - it depends on your city, rate of return, and discipline to actually invest the savings.

Licences are granted by category, according to what the FSP does:

  • Category I - advice and/or intermediary services (the most common; ordinary advisors).
  • Category II - discretionary FSPs (make investment decisions for clients without prior approval each time).
  • Category IIA - hedge fund FSPs.
  • Category III - administrative FSPs (e.g. LISPs / investment administration).
  • Category IV - assistance business FSPs.

An FSP is licensed only for the categories and product subcategories it applied for and was approved for.

Life insurance policies follow the Insurance Act, not the Pension Funds Act. Here, your nominated beneficiary has a binding contractual right, the insurer pays them directly, bypassing your estate.

Estate-duty implications:

  • Policies with nominated beneficiaries: included in estate duty calculation BUT the estate duty liability can be reduced by the 'Section 3(3)(a) deduction'
  • In practice: the first R3.5 million of life insurance to the estate is duty-free (part of the general abatement)

Common mistake: Naming your estate as life policy beneficiary (instead of a person). This means the payout goes into your estate, becomes available to creditors, and takes 12-24 months to reach your family. Name a person, not 'my estate'.

The fix: when you get a raise, commit to saving at least 50% of the increase before upgrading anything.

This asymmetry drives irrational financial decisions: holding losing investments too long, selling winning investments too early, and paying excessive insurance for unlikely events.

Many business owners take money out as a 'loan' from their company to avoid both salary tax and dividends tax. SARS closed this loophole with Section 7C.

Section 7C rules (from 2017): If your Pty Ltd or trust lends money to you (a connected person) at below the official interest rate (currently repo rate = 7.75%), the difference is a deemed donation. Donations Tax of 20% applies on amounts above R100 000 donated per year.

Example: Pty Ltd lends you R1 000 000 at 0% interest. Notional interest at 7.75% = R77 500. After R100 000 annual exclusion, nothing taxable this year. But the loan grows, by year 3, notional interest cumulates. SARS expects either the loan to be repaid or the notional interest declared.

  • Use guaranteed annuity to cover essential monthly expenses (rent/bond, food, utilities, medical aid)
  • Use living annuity for discretionary spending and estate planning

This gives: longevity certainty for basics (guaranteed) + flexibility for extras + potential estate value (living). The Sanlam 'annuity umbrella' and similar products offer this structure.

Many salaried employees don't need to file. PAYE handles it and SARS may auto-assess. But you generally must file if you're self-employed, have more than one income source, have taxable benefits not fully taxed via PAYE, earn investment or rental income, want to claim deductions (RA, medical, home office), or SARS asks you to.

Provisional tax: earn more than R30 000/year from non-salary sources and you register as a provisional taxpayer, submitting estimates twice a year (August and February). Late filing carries monthly penalties. Filing correctly and on time is always cheaper than ignoring it.

Many South Africans who leave the country permanently still file as SA residents, creating ongoing tax obligations they are unaware of. Formally ceasing tax residency triggers:

  • Deemed disposal: SARS treats all your worldwide assets as sold on the day you leave. CGT is payable on all unrealised gains.
  • Retirement fund exit tax: If you withdraw your pension or RA after formal emigration, a different tax table applies (lump sum tables, not normal income tax).
  • Future SA income: You will pay non-resident tax on SA-source income at withholding rates (15% on interest, 20% dividends tax).

Ceasing residency is often a net benefit for high-net-worth individuals with significant offshore assets, but must be planned carefully with a tax professional. The 'exit tax' on deemed disposal is payable regardless, but is a one-time cost vs ongoing worldwide income tax.

Markowitz's Nobel-winning insight: combining assets that don't move together can cut a portfolio's risk without sacrificing much return, the closest thing to a free lunch. The key is low correlation: when the JSE falls, global holdings (helped by a weaker rand) may cushion the blow.

Asset allocation (the split between SA equities, global equities, bonds and cash) explains over 90% of long-term variability; stock picking and timing explain under 10%. And rebalancing back to target systematically sells what rose and buys what lagged.

Mental accounting is the tendency to treat money differently depending on where it came from or what we mentally label it. A tax refund feels like 'free money' and is spent impulsively. Regular salary is budgeted carefully. But R10 000 is R10 000 regardless of whether it came from SARS, a bonus, or a gift.

Mental accounting causes people to simultaneously: spend casino winnings frivolously, keep debt at 22% interest while holding savings at 5%, or invest a bonus but not regular income.

Most South Africans are underinsured. The question isn't whether to have life cover, but how much.

The 10× rule: a common starting point is 10× your annual salary. Earn R30 000/month (R360 000/year) and that's about R3.6 million.

More precise: add up outstanding debt, children's education, the years of income to replace, and final costs. A common target is to replace about 75% of your net income. Review it every couple of years. Cover taken out at 25 is usually too little at 35.

This is why cash under the mattress is a slow leak: it loses buying power every single year.

Oil is priced in dollars, so the petrol price depends on both the oil price and the exchange rate. Petrol can rise even when oil falls. The Basic Fuel Price is only one component: the general fuel levy, the RAF levy, wholesale and retail margins and transport all sit on top, and the levies are set in the Budget. Fuel reaches even non-drivers through taxi fares and food prices, which is why increases hit low-income households hardest.

  • If rates fall 1% to 10.75%: ≈ R10 600/month - R500 less - R6 000/year saved

Every 1% rate change on a R1m bond = approximately R500/month = R6 000/year.

Phishing is when criminals send fake emails or SMSes pretending to be your bank, SARS or a trusted company. The goal: get you to click a link and hand over your details.

Red flags: urgent threats ('account closes in 24 hours!'); a generic 'Dear Customer'; a free-email sender (absa.support@gmail.com is NOT Absa); lookalike links (www.absa-secure.co.za). The golden rule: no real bank ever asks for your PIN, password or OTP, and when in doubt, contact the bank yourself using your app or a number you look up, never the one in the message.

Profit is recorded when you invoice; cash arrives when clients pay. That gap is why profitable businesses run out of money and close, and growth makes it worse, because every new order consumes cash before it produces any. Deposits upfront are standard practice and the cheapest working capital there is. A simple rolling weekly cash forecast tells you which weeks you'll be short, early enough to do something about it.

Psychological research consistently shows people spend windfall income (bonuses, tax refunds, inheritances) more freely than regular income, even when they have outstanding debt or savings goals.

A December bonus of R15 000 that gets spent on a TV and holiday in two weeks is not 'extra money'. It's income that could have:

  • Paid off a credit card at 22%
  • Been invested in an ETF compounding at 10%+ over 20 years
  • Funded three months of emergency savings

Fix: Before receiving a bonus, decide in advance what percentage goes to debt repayment, savings, and spending. The commitment before the money arrives prevents the mental accounting trap from activating.

Research by Brinson, Hood, and Beebower found that over 90% of long-term portfolio return variability is explained by asset allocation, the split between asset classes, not by which specific shares or funds you pick.

The five main asset classes in a SA investor's toolkit:

  • Equities (shares): Highest long-term return, highest short-term volatility. JSE, global shares.
  • Bonds (fixed income): Moderate return, lower volatility. Government and corporate bonds.
  • Property (REITs): Income + capital growth. Retail, office, industrial property.
  • Cash: Lowest return, zero volatility. Money market, fixed deposits.
  • Alternatives: Commodities, hedge funds (generally inaccessible to retail investors).

The right allocation depends on your time horizon and risk tolerance, not on market conditions today.

Retirement funds (pension, provident, RA) are governed by the Pension Funds Act Section 37C. The trustee board of your fund must consider all financial dependants, not just your nominees.

If you nominate only your spouse but you have three minor children from a previous relationship who depend on you financially, the trustees may distribute part of the benefit to those children regardless of your nomination.

Practical rule: Name all financial dependants as nominees in proportion to their dependency. Update nominations annually and after every life event. The fund administrator provides nomination forms, ask for them today.

SA has tax treaties with 80+ countries to prevent the same income being taxed twice. The relief works in two ways:

Exemption method: One country gives up its right to tax. Example: SA-UK treaty, SA residents earning UK rental income may pay UK tax and receive a SA exemption (less common).

Credit method (more common): SA taxes the income but credits foreign tax paid. If the UK deducts 20% tax on R200 000 rental (R40 000), and your SA liability on that income is R90 000, you pay only R50 000 more to SARS.

Dividend withholding tax: When your US ETF pays dividends, the US withholds 30% (15% under treaty if you file W-8BEN). This foreign withholding tax is credited against your SA income tax on those dividends. Your SA broker (EasyEquities, Ninety One) handles the W-8BEN form.

SARS gives individuals two major CGT shields:

Annual exclusion: R40 000. The first R40 000 of capital gains or losses is ignored every year. On death, this rises to R300 000.

Primary residence exclusion: R2 million, Gain on selling your main home. If you sell for R3.5m and bought for R1.2m (gain = R2.3m), only R300 000 is taxable after the R2m exclusion. The property must have been your primary residence and used mainly for residential purposes.

Combined, a long-time homeowner in the 45% bracket on a R2.3m gain pays CGT on only R260 000 after both exclusions, effective tax of approximately R46 800, not R207 000 on the full gain.

SARS takes exactly what you owe, but won't tell you about the legal ways to pay less. Employees who don't know about RA deductions, medical credits and home-office deductions overpay by thousands every year.

SA uses marginal tax brackets: you only pay the higher rate on income above each threshold, never on your whole salary. For 2026/27, under-65s pay no tax below R99 000 (the primary rebate of R17 820 cancels it), and the top marginal rate is 45%. The myth that a raise can cut your take-home is impossible. You always keep more by earning more.

SARS taxes trusts punitively to prevent wealthy individuals from parking income in trusts at lower rates:

  • Income retained in trust: Taxed at a flat 45%, the same as the highest individual bracket
  • Capital gains in trust: 80% inclusion rate × 45% = effective 36%
  • Income vested (paid out) to beneficiaries: Taxed in the beneficiary's hands at their rate

The planning opportunity: If you have adult children or a spouse in lower tax brackets, vesting income from the trust to them is taxed at their rate (potentially 18% or 26%), not 45%. This is legal income-splitting and can save significant tax annually.

See a debit order you never authorised? SA banking rules entitle you to a reversal.

  • You have 60 days from the debit date to dispute it as unauthorised.
  • Contact your bank (app, call centre or branch) and formally dispute it.
  • DebiCheck mandates you never approved are reversed without fuss; contested ones can take up to ~10 business days.

Keep screenshots and reference numbers. If a company keeps debiting after a reversal, escalate free to the National Financial Ombud (NFO) (0860 800 900). Watch for small recurring amounts (R19, R49, R99), the classic subscription scam.

Sell an asset (shares, property, unit trusts, crypto) for more than you paid and the profit is a capital gain, taxed via CGT. For individuals: a R50 000 annual exclusion (you only count gains above it), then a 40% inclusion rate (40% of the net gain is added to your taxable income). At the top 45% marginal rate that's an 18% effective maximum.

Your primary residence gets a R3 000 000 exclusion (2026/27), which is why most people pay no CGT selling their home. Example: buy shares for R50 000, sell for R120 000 → R70 000 gain, less R50 000 exclusion = R20 000, of which 40% (R8 000) is added to income. And inside a TFSA, capital gains are tax-free entirely.

Nobody forecasts currencies reliably; a steady allocation beats timing.

South Africa taxes residents on their worldwide income, not just income earned in SA. If you live in SA, your dividends from a US ETF, your rental income from a UK flat, and your freelance income from a Swiss client are all taxable by SARS.

You are a SA tax resident if:

  • You are ordinarily resident in SA (your real home is here), OR
  • You were physically in SA for 91 days in the current year and 549 days in the past 5 years

Many South Africans working abroad incorrectly believe they have stopped being tax residents simply by leaving. Formal tax emigration (changing your tax status to non-resident) is a separate legal process with significant implications.

South Africa uses residence-based taxation: if you're an SA tax resident, your worldwide income is taxable here. Non-residents are taxed only on SA-source income.

Two big reliefs for residents working abroad: the foreign employment exemption (s10(1)(o)(ii)), up to R1.25 million of foreign salary is exempt if you spend more than 183 days abroad (including a continuous 60-day stretch) in a 12-month period, and foreign tax credits (s6quat), which offset tax already paid overseas so the same income isn't taxed twice.

Claiming real deductions is legal tax planning; hiding income is illegal evasion. Keep your certificates and receipts.

The FAIS Ombud (the Ombud for Financial Services Providers) resolves complaints by clients against FSPs/representatives fairly, economically and expeditiously. The Ombud can investigate, mediate and make a determination that has the effect of a court order.

The Ombud's monetary jurisdiction is limited: it may award compensation up to R3.5 million for a single complaint (a complainant may abandon the amount above this to stay within jurisdiction).

Note: the Ombud Council Rules that took effect on 1 July 2024 raised this limit from R800 000 to R3 500 000. Older study material still quotes R800 000 - the current figure is R3.5 million.

  • Keep records; and train staff.

The real interest rate = nominal rate - inflation rate. This is what your money actually earns after inflation erodes purchasing power.

Example: Your savings account pays 9%. Inflation is 5.5%. Your real return is 3.5%, that's how much your wealth is actually growing in purchasing-power terms.

Negative real rates: If inflation exceeds your savings rate, your purchasing power shrinks even while your rand balance grows. In 2020-2021, SA real rates were near zero or negative, cash was quietly losing value.

For long-term wealth building, you need assets that consistently beat inflation over time. That's the core argument for investing in equities rather than keeping all savings in cash.

The repo rate (repurchase rate) is the interest rate at which the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) lends money overnight to commercial banks. It is the most powerful lever the SARB uses to manage inflation in SA.

The repo rate sets the floor for all interest rates in the economy. Every mortgage, car loan, credit card, and savings account in South Africa is ultimately priced relative to it.

2024 context: The repo rate was 8.25% for most of 2024. The SARB cut it to 8.0% in September 2024 and again to 7.75% in November 2024, the first cuts since 2020, when COVID drove rates to historic lows of 3.5%.

The repo rate is what the SARB charges banks. Prime = repo + 3.5%, and prime moves point for point with it, so a 0.25% cut lowers a variable bond by exactly 0.25%. Every decision moves money between borrowers and savers: rate rises hurt anyone with a bond and help anyone with deposits. Rates affect inflation by cooling demand, and the effect arrives with a lag of many months.

Fixed rates buy certainty at a premium; variable wins when rates fall. Paying extra capital shrinks the balance future interest is charged on.

The 4% safe withdrawal rate comes from US research (Trinity Study, 1998) on US markets over 30 years. In SA, the picture is more complex:

  • Higher inflation: SA's long-run CPI averages 5-6% vs US 2-3%. The 4% rule needs inflation adjustment.
  • Higher bond yields: SA bonds yield more, which helps income portfolios
  • Currency volatility: Rand depreciation affects purchasing power for imported goods
  • JSE volatility: Higher than most developed markets

Practical SA guidance: Financial advisors suggest 3-3.5% initial withdrawal rate for SA retirees with a 30-year horizon, rising to 4-4.5% if the portfolio has significant offshore exposure (which acts as a natural inflation and rand-weakness hedge).

Open a case with SAPS (10111) if theft occurred. Some recovery paths need a case number. Follow your bank's affidavit process, and ask which ombudsman or regulator handles your product type.

When you might move within a few years (transaction costs take years to recover), when your deposit could earn more invested elsewhere, in a high price-to-rent city, when you value flexibility, or when buying would stretch you dangerously thin.

The idea that renting is "throwing money away" is one of the most damaging myths in personal finance. Renting is often the smarter financial choice depending on your circumstances.

Renting makes sense when:

  • You plan to move within 3-5 years (transaction costs of buying take years to break even)
  • Your deposit money is better invested elsewhere (equity at 12% vs property at 6-8% per year)
  • You are in a city with a high price-to-rent ratio (buying is expensive relative to renting)
  • You value flexibility - for career opportunities, relationship changes, or lifestyle
  • You cannot yet afford a property without stretching yourself dangerously thin

Opportunity cost of your deposit: R200 000 in a deposit reduces your loan and interest. But R200 000 invested in a diversified equity fund at 12%/year grows to R620 000 in 10 years. The question is always: which use of that capital creates more wealth?

Rental yield perspective: If annual rent is R84 000 (R7 000/month) on a property worth R1 500 000, the yield is 5.6%. Investors who buy to let often earn less than 6% yield - sometimes less than you would in a money market account.

The landmark Brinson, Hood and Beebower study (1986, replicated multiple times) found that asset allocation (the split between equities, bonds, property, cash and offshore) explains over 90% of long-term portfolio variability. Stock picking and market timing together explain less than 10%.

Practical implication: The decision 'how much in SA equities vs global equities vs bonds vs cash?' matters far more than which specific fund or ETF you choose. Getting the allocation right, and keeping costs low within each allocation, is the core of long-term wealth building.

SA-specific context: Many SA investors are heavily overweight SA assets (JSE All Share, SA property, SA bonds). SA represents less than 0.5% of global GDP. A 100% SA portfolio is a concentrated bet on one emerging market.

The most tax-efficient strategy for most owner-managed Pty Ltd businesses:

  1. Pay yourself a salary equal to roughly the top of the 31% bracket (approx R480 000/year in 2024/25). This maximises RA deductions and medical credits against a moderate rate.
  2. Take additional profits as dividends (27% corporate tax + 20% DT = ~41.6% effective).
  3. Maximise RA contributions from the salary, up to 27.5% deducted before income tax.

Example: Business makes R1.2m profit. Pay R480 000 salary, contribute R132 000 to RA (27.5%). Taxable salary = R348 000, tax ≈ R87 000. Remaining R720 000 profit: company pays R194 400 corporate tax, declares R525 600 dividend, you pay R105 120 DT. Total tax = R386 520 on R1.2m vs R540 000 if all taken as salary at 45%.

The MPC meets six times a year and has one primary mandate: keep CPI inflation within a 3-6% target band.

When inflation rises above 6%: The MPC raises the repo rate. Higher rates make borrowing expensive, reduce consumer spending, and cool inflation. Side effect: growth slows, unemployment may rise.

When inflation falls or growth weakens: The MPC cuts the repo rate. Cheaper borrowing stimulates spending, investment, and economic growth. Side effect: if cut too aggressively, inflation can reignite.

The MPC must balance inflation control against economic growth, it's always a trade-off. SA's 2022-2024 rate hike cycle (from 3.5% to 8.25% over 18 months) was the most aggressive in 15 years, triggered by post-COVID supply shocks and global rate hikes.

The phrase 'guaranteed returns' is the most reliable sign of a scam in investing. Any product promising a fixed return well above the risk-free rate (a few percent, roughly in line with prevailing interest rates) is almost certainly fraudulent, because real returns above that come with real risk. Ponzi schemes 'guarantee' it by paying early investors with later investors' money, until they collapse.

How to check: any investment offered to the public must be run by an FSCA-licensed provider. Verify on the FSCA register at fsca.co.za before you invest a cent, and report suspected scams to the FSCA (0800 110 443).

The transmission works in three steps:

  1. Repo rate: Set by the SARB Monetary Policy Committee (MPC). Currently 7.75% (end 2024).
  2. Prime lending rate: Commercial banks add 3.5 percentage points. Prime = repo + 3.5%. At repo 7.75%, prime = 11.25%.
  3. Your rate: Banks lend to you at prime minus or plus a spread based on your risk profile. A good home loan might be prime - 0.5% = 10.75%. A risky personal loan could be prime + 8% = 19.25%.

When the MPC raises or cuts the repo rate, prime moves by exactly the same amount, and every variable-rate debt or deposit in the country is repriced immediately.
