Key checks: the current ratio (below 1 is a liquidity risk), debtor days (rising = customers paying too slowly), and EBITDA margin (operating profit before interest, tax and non-cash charges). Above all. Profit is not cash. Profitable businesses fail by running out of cash.

  • Sole Proprietor: No registration needed. Simple. But personal and business liability are the same - creditors can claim personal assets.
  • Private Company (Pty Ltd): CIPC registration ~R175 online. Separate legal entity - limited personal liability. More admin (annual returns, financial statements). Better for growth.
  • Partnership: Simple but joint and several liability - each partner is liable for ALL business debts.

Time horizon is the most important variable in choosing an investment:

  • 0-3 years: Cash, money market only - can't afford a market downturn
  • 3-7 years: Balanced funds, bonds + some equities
  • 7-15 years: 70-80% equities
  • 15+ years: 80-100% equities

Start reducing equity exposure 5 years before your goal date.

Two payslip lines most people ignore: UIF and SDL.

UIF: you pay 1% of salary (up to a R17 712/month earnings cap, so at most R177.12), your employer pays another 1%. Lose your job, get retrenched, or go on maternity leave, and you can claim a portion of your income for a limited period.

SDL (Skills Development Levy): your employer pays 1% of payroll to the SETAs to fund training. You do not pay this. It's an employer cost, so it never appears as a deduction on your payslip.

Two retirees can have the same average return yet very different outcomes, because the order of returns matters once you're withdrawing income. A crash early in retirement forces you to sell units at low prices, and that capital never shares in the recovery. This is sequence-of-returns risk.

SA's higher inflation argues for a cautious starting withdrawal rate (3-3.5%, up to 4-4.5% with offshore exposure). Defences: a 1-2 year cash buffer, a bucket strategy, and cutting withdrawals in bad years so you never have to sell equities at the bottom.

Two types of insurance protect a home. Buildings insurance covers the structure (walls, roof, fitted kitchen, plumbing) paying to rebuild after fire, storm or a burst geyser. If you have a bond, your bank usually requires it. Contents insurance covers your furniture, appliances, electronics and valuables inside.

In sectional-title, the body corporate usually insures the structure, so you still need contents cover. Watch the exclusions: gradual wear and tear is generally not covered, and an aging, rusted geyser may be excluded. Check the wording.

When making any portfolio change, ask two questions before acting:

1. Does this move me toward or away from my target allocation?
Any change should serve your stated strategy. 'This share looks interesting' is not a portfolio reason.

2. What is the after-tax, after-cost return of this decision?
A 12% fund with 2.5% annual fee nets 9.5%. A 10.5% fund with 0.3% fee nets 10.2%. High-cost products can only justify their fees if they consistently outperform by more than the fee difference, which very few active funds do.

Fee compounding works against you: R100 000 at 10% over 30 years = R1 745 000. At 9% (1% higher fee) = R1 327 000. That 1% fee difference costs R418 000 over 30 years.

When you buy a share on the JSE, you buy part-ownership of a listed company. If it grows profits and pays dividends, you can earn from both a rising price and the payouts. If the business struggles, your slice can lose value. That's normal market behaviour, not necessarily fraud.

Many beginners start with broad ETFs holding dozens or hundreds of companies, so one bad decision at one firm doesn't dominate the outcome. Outside a TFSA you still pay tax, so wrapping long-term equity ETFs inside your annual TFSA limit can make sense when the rules allow.

When your Pty Ltd makes a profit, there are three main ways to take money out. Salary: deductible for the company, taxed in your hands at up to 45%. Dividend: paid from after-tax profit, 27% company tax, then 20% dividends withholding tax, about 41.6% combined. Loan account: allowed, but must carry interest at the official rate (s7C), so it's not a long-term plan.

At the very top bracket a dividend edges out a salary (≈R58.40 vs ≈R55 per R100 of profit), but lower down a salary using rebates and lower brackets often wins, so most owners use a mix.

When your Pty Ltd makes a profit, you have three ways to get money out:

  1. Salary: Taxed in your hands at marginal rates (up to 45%). Tax-deductible for the company. Creates UIF and pension obligations.
  2. Dividend: Paid from after-tax company profits. Company pays 27% corporate tax, then 20% Dividends Tax, effectively 41.6% total. No UIF, no pension obligation.
  3. Loan account: Draw money as a loan to yourself. Interest must be charged at repo rate (SARS Section 7C). Not a long-term solution.

For a business owner in the 45% marginal bracket, a salary costing the company R100 000 delivers R55 000 in hand. A dividend: company earns R100 000, pays R27 000 tax → R73 000, then 20% DT → R58 400 in hand. Dividend wins by R3 400 per R100 000 at the top bracket.

You are entitled to one free credit report per year from each credit bureau under the National Credit Act. SA credit bureaus: TransUnion, Experian, Compuscan (now Experian), and XDS.

Free checks: ClearScore (free monthly updates, Experian data) and annualcreditreport.co.za.

What to look for on your report:

  • Payment history on each account, any missed payments?
  • Adverse listings (judgements, defaults, debt review status)
  • Accounts you don't recognise, potential fraud
  • Enquiries, who has searched your credit in the last 12 months?
  • Balances and limits on all credit accounts

Dispute errors: Creditors must remove incorrect adverse information within 20 business days of being notified. One incorrect listing can suppress your score for years.

  • 'Experience budgets' give lasting joy; 'object budgets' often don't

Your business may be your largest asset. You can't sell it, buy out a partner, raise equity, or plan your estate fairly without knowing its worth. The most common method for an operating business is EBITDA × an industry multiple (SA SMEs often 2-5×, versus 8-15× for listed companies). Other methods: discounted cash flow (rigorous but assumption-sensitive) and net asset value (a floor for asset-heavy businesses).

What kills a valuation: all fixable before a sale: customer concentration, owner-dependence, messy books, and no written contracts.

Your credit score (300-850 in SA) is calculated from five weighted factors. Understanding each gives you a blueprint to build or rebuild your score:

  • Payment History (~35%): The single biggest factor. Every on-time payment improves it. Every missed or late payment damages it, and stays on record for up to 7 years.
  • Credit Utilisation (~30%): How much of your available credit you use. Using R9 000 of a R10 000 credit card limit = 90% utilisation. This signals financial stress to lenders. Keep utilisation below 30%, ideally below 10%.
  • Length of Credit History (~15%): Older accounts improve your score. Don't close your oldest credit card even if unused, length of history matters.
  • Credit Mix (~10%): Having different types of credit (home loan, credit card, store card) shows you can manage complexity. But don't open accounts just for mix.
  • New Applications (~10%): Each credit application triggers a 'hard inquiry' which slightly drops your score. Multiple applications in a short period signals desperation.

Your executor administers your estate after death: collects assets, pays debts, pays estate duty, and distributes to beneficiaries. This process can take 1-3 years.

Options:

  • Family member: Possible if they are competent. Must appoint an agent (attorney or bank trust) if the estate exceeds R250 000. Not practical for complex estates.
  • Attorney or financial advisor: Negotiate fees upfront. Statutory maximum is 3.5% + VAT of gross estate value, but many accept less, especially if the estate is large and straightforward.
  • Bank trust company: Reliable but impersonal, and typically charges the full 3.5%.

Practical action: Name your executor in your will and negotiate their fee in writing before you die. For a R5 million estate, the difference between 3.5% (R202 750) and 1% (R57 930) is R144 820: preserved for your family.

Your will controls your estate. But several major assets bypass your estate entirely if you have named beneficiaries, your will cannot override these nominations.

Assets that pass via beneficiary nomination (not your will):

  • Pension, provident, and retirement annuity funds
  • Group life insurance through your employer
  • Individual life policies where you named a beneficiary

Why this matters: If your will says 'everything to my children equally' but your pension fund says 'ex-spouse', your ex-spouse gets the pension. Courts have confirmed this repeatedly. Beneficiary nominations must be reviewed at every major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of children, death of a nominee.

Zandile puts R2 500 a month into a normal unit trust outside a TFSA. Over the years she owes tax on some interest, dividends and capital gains. Her twin uses the same funds inside a TFSA wrapper (within the limits) and keeps more of the compounding, because qualifying growth isn't taxed.

TFSAs still have annual (R46 000) and lifetime (R500 000) caps; over-contributing triggers a 40% SARS penalty. Regular taxable accounts have no caps but no shelter. Many people use both: the TFSA for long-term wealth, a plain account for flexibility beyond the limits.
